title: Othello
author: William Shakespeare
about:
Othello is a Moorish general in the service of Venice who has secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a Venetian senator. His ensign, Iago, has been passed over for promotion and decides to destroy him. Iago insinuates, with no real evidence, that Desdemona is sleeping with Cassio, the lieutenant who got the post Iago wanted. He plants a handkerchief, stages a conversation Othello half-overhears, and works on him until Othello murders Desdemona in their bed. The truth comes out moments after she is dead. Othello kills himself on the same bed.

Shakespeare wrote the play around 1603, drawing on a short Italian novella by Cinthio. He gave Iago twice as many lines as Othello and let the audience watch the whole machinery from inside Iago's head while Othello, on stage, sees nothing. The play ran in Jacobean London under the new king James and survived four centuries of debate about who exactly Othello is — Moor, Black African, Berber, soldier, husband, hero, gullible fool — and what Shakespeare meant by putting him at the centre of a love story that ends in a strangling.

Of the four major tragedies, Othello is the most claustrophobic and the most domestic. There are no ghosts, no witches, no battle scenes after the opening — only two people in a bedroom, a handkerchief, and a man who has been talked into believing the worst.

angleCards.title: Iago's motive.
angleCards.text: Iago gives three different reasons for hating Othello — being passed over for promotion, a rumour that Othello slept with his wife, and pure dislike — and never settles on one. Coleridge called this 'motiveless malignity.' Track what he actually says and decide for yourself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to track every reason Iago gives for hating Othello and decide whether he has a real motive or whether the cruelty is its own end.

angleCards.title: How fast it happens.
angleCards.text: Iago plants the first seed of suspicion at the start of Act 3. By the end of Act 3, Othello is calling for blood. The play is partly an experiment in how quickly a sane, capable man can be talked into murder.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Othello as a study in psychological persuasion: how Iago moves Othello from love to murder in under three hours of stage time.

angleCards.title: Desdemona.
angleCards.text: Desdemona has no flaw the play actually shows. She marries Othello against her father's wishes, defends her choice in front of the Venetian senate, follows him to Cyprus, and dies asking forgiveness for her own murder. Watch what the play does and does not give her.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Desdemona as the play's quietest figure — what she chooses, what she does not get to choose, and how Shakespeare handles a wife who never actually does what she is killed for.

angleCards.title: Race in the play.
angleCards.text: Othello is described by Iago and Roderigo as 'the Moor,' 'thick-lips,' 'old black ram.' Othello himself names his colour in his last speech. The play is the first major work in English literature to take a Black man as its tragic hero, and it has been argued about ever since.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Othello with attention to how race functions in the play — what the other characters say about him, what he says about himself, and what the tragedy depends on.

cast.name: Othello
cast.description: A Black general in the service of the Venetian state, recently and secretly married to Desdemona. He has spent his life on campaign, won his place by service, and is the most decorated soldier in Venice. He loves his wife with an intensity that turns into something else the moment doubt enters. The play is the inside of a man who has nothing to fall back on but his honour and is helped to throw it away.

cast.name: Iago
cast.description: Othello's standard-bearer, passed over for the lieutenancy in favour of Cassio. He addresses the audience directly more than any other Shakespeare villain and lets us watch him invent each new lie. He has more lines than Othello and is one of the most fully developed antagonists in English drama.

cast.name: Desdemona
cast.description: The daughter of the Venetian senator Brabantio, recently eloped with Othello. She is intelligent, brave, and devoted; she defends her marriage in front of the Senate and follows Othello to Cyprus. She does not do, and never considers doing, what Iago accuses her of.

cast.name: Cassio
cast.description: The young officer Othello promotes over Iago at the start of the play. He is charming, educated, and friendly with Desdemona — which is enough, with Iago's help, to make him a target.

cast.name: Emilia
cast.description: Iago's wife and Desdemona's maid. She finds the lost handkerchief and gives it to Iago without knowing what it is for. In the final scene she works out what her husband has done and refuses to be silent about it, no matter what it costs.

cast.name: Roderigo
cast.description: A wealthy Venetian gentleman in love with Desdemona. He pays Iago to help him win her and is strung along through the entire play, used as a knife when Iago needs one and disposed of when he is no longer useful.

acclaim.quote: Othello, Iago, Desdemona, Emilia, are all in [Shakespeare's] phrase, 'extant, and writ in choice Italian'; we cannot conceive of the play apart from them.
The motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity — how awful it is!
acclaim.context: marginal note on Iago, in Coleridge's Notes and Lectures upon Shakespeare, published 1849

whyItMatters.title: The Inventor of Modern Manipulation
whyItMatters.body: Iago does what later villains in literature and film have done ever since: he never tells Othello a direct lie. He plants a question, lets Othello answer it, and refuses to confirm what he has just made him think. 'Ha! I like not that' as Cassio leaves Desdemona is not a statement; it is an opening Othello fills himself. The handkerchief works the same way — Iago drops it where it will be found, and lets the world decide what it means. Almost every fictional manipulator since works in some version of this mode, from Henry James's governesses to John le Carré's case officers to the antagonists of Hitchcock and Patricia Highsmith. The play built the template four centuries ago and has not been improved on.

whyItMatters.title: The Speed of Belief
whyItMatters.body: Othello opens Act 3 happily married. By the end of Act 3 he is on his knees swearing to kill his wife. The play compresses what looks, on paper, like an impossibly fast moral collapse into something a sane man can follow scene by scene. Each step Iago takes is small: a question, a reluctance to speak, a half-quoted rumour. Each step Othello takes is just slightly bigger: a worry, then a demand for proof, then a willingness to accept proof too thin. Shakespeare is doing what cognitive psychologists would later call confirmation bias and what con artists have always known: once a man wants to believe something, he will accept evidence he would otherwise have laughed at. The tragedy is not that Othello is stupid. The tragedy is that he is exactly as smart as the rest of us under the same conditions.

whyItMatters.title: The First Black Tragic Hero in English
whyItMatters.body: Othello is the first major work in English literature to put a Black man at the centre of its sympathy and its grief. The play was performed for the first time at the court of James I, who had just become king of a country that had perhaps a few hundred Africans living in it; almost no one in the audience would have spoken to a Moor in their lives. Shakespeare gives him the most musical verse in the play, makes him a more accomplished general than any of the Venetians around him, and lets him deliver — twice — the most dignified speeches in his own tragedy. He also lets Iago and Brabantio and Roderigo use the worst language available to them, and lets Othello fall into the trap that has been set partly by his own race. The play has been argued about for four centuries and will go on being argued about: it is the place where the question entered English literature and has never quite left.
